When it came to Latif, the main character played by Mahershala Ali, Gowan knew she had to embrace the character’s contradictions. “This is a man who is battling his faith,” Gowan said. “I wanted to be very mindful and respectful of Muslim identity, but not fall into a prescribed idea of what a Muslim is, because there is no such thing. But there is a construct of Black Muslim style and contemporary modern life,  an unabashed way of dress that is vibrant, that is rich in texture, that is rich in color and swag.”

Gowan drew upon a wide array of influences for Latif’s clothes, referencing Tuareg (particularly in the indigo color palette) and Baye Fall African warriors, as well as the more utilitarian aspects of Japanese samurai clothing. “I had to maintain a balance, because this character’s everyday life is as a father,” Gowan said, “but when we first meet him we’re introduced to him as a killer. We don’t know his backstory. So there’s a level of restraint that’s very important — I didn’t want the costumes to announce themselves.”

Several of Latif’s costumes were original designs Gowan created to reflect his daily life and emotional state. “For the funeral scene, I designed his thobe to combine a traditional tunic silhouette with the details of a tailored men’s dress shirt: micro-stripe shirting with a contrasting denim band collar and cuffs. I also designed the loose shalwar trousers in blue and white that he wears during his meditative practice with his sword. His multicolored morning tunic, with its long sleeves, reflects his attempt at optimism. Across these looks, the untucked shirts, long sleeves, and loose trousers maintain the modesty and ease that ground his everyday looks, while the individual details express different aspects of his character.”

Latif’s duality becomes especially clear in his long denim kimono coat, which Gowan created in collaboration with Daisuke Muramatsu, owner of Prospective Flow, using pieces from his collection. “It brings the warrior influences of my research into Latif’s contemporary assassin look while remaining rooted in his everyday wardrobe,” Gowan said. “The addition of his Tuareg-inspired tagelmust and the embossed leather belt holding his sword sheath changes its function and how we read him. Latif remains a father, a man of faith, and a warrior throughout that seamless transition.”

While Latif represents one approach to faith and violence, his adversary Pastor Hwan (John Cho) represents another. An evangelist cult leader in charge of a heavily armed militia, Hwan is as sincere in his beliefs as Latif is in his — and seems completely unaware of the even greater contradictions between his faith as he preaches it and his actions in practice. “My research really began with cult leaders and how they are able to draw people in,” Gowan said. “How do they identify in their dress and style?”

In addition to real-life cult and religious leaders, Gowan was influenced by the look of the John Hawkes character in “Martha Marcy May Marlene.” She then honed in on the look of militias, always with an eye on the Houston locale. “The cowboy hat was crucial,” she said. “He needed something that didn’t just sit on his head, but was subtle. The costume was very much about the details, like the iconography of crosses on the jeans. John was still searching for who the character was, and when he stepped into the fitting room, he was transformed.”

Gowan was particularly interested in how the character could use clothing to project authority and command attention. “I drew on Texas and Western iconography: the cowboy hat, boots, spurs, embellished denim, and prominent eye-catching details. The hat and boots give him an assertive, immediately recognizable silhouette. His outward display contrasts with the restraint of Latif’s everyday look.”

Hwan’s most arresting piece of clothing is a shirt he wears that Gowan bought in a store but then completely embellished. “On a Friday evening I got a note, ‘Hey, we want to do some kind of portrait of his mother or something on the back of his shirt,'” Gowan said. “This had to be on camera Monday, and we needed six multiples.  I had to set about finding an airbrush artist who could hand paint and turn around some type of image of a mother in a very short amount of time, on top of embellishing the shirts.”

Fringe details and studs were added to the shirt’s placket and color, with everything coming together in a 72-hour period. “When you’re on a project like this, it’s a very short time frame,” Gowan said, noting that she only had one fitting with each of her lead actors. Luckily, her extensive research and attention to detail paid off. “When we tried all the final pieces on that day and John stepped out of his camper fully loaded with the cowboy hat in his hand, the jeans, the shirt, the black ostrich boots with the spurs, and the belt buckle with crosses on it, it just came together.”

For the film’s third key character, Latif’s daughter Fatiha (Adia), Gowan had to represent yet another approach to faith, with less latitude for overt stylization than in Latif or Pastor Hwan. “ Fatiha is somewhat wise beyond her years,” Gowan said. “She’s finding herself. She’s trying to understand who she is as a young girl who has to grow up relatively quickly, and handle a lot of responsibility for her younger brother and her newly born sister. I wanted to show a young Muslim girl’s freedom of expression through her clothing.”

With that in mind, Gowan’s research for Fatiha brought modest yet modern teenage silhouettes into conversation with roomy streetwear, track jackets, sports jerseys, sneakers, and expressive layering. One key to Gowan’s approach was the way she handled the character’s hijabs. “Her colorful hijabs were tied and styled in various ways, giving her costumes a language of comfort and a controlled sense of teenage rebellion,” Gowan said. “Her palette made room for rich mustard yellows, muted greens and blues, and lavender hues.”

Gowan was also sure to use Fatiha’s look as a point of comparison and contrast with her father. “I wanted to portray the fact that she was youthful, she was vibrant, but she was also a rebel,” Gowan said. “She was questioning her father in very direct ways, so it was important that she had an aesthetic that was very much her own. The color and silhouette gave her a different energy from her father while keeping her a formidable presence within the same grounded cultural world. Their costumes express different generations and points of view within the faith, community, and intimate family space they share.”

As with the other characters, Gowan wanted Fatiha’s clothes to convey inner conflict. “There are moments where she’s just very pared down and very simple in the home,” Gowan said, adding that one of her favorite looks comes in a scene where Fatiha steals milk for her baby sister. “She’s got this hockey jersey on, and she’s got her jeans, and she’s got her hijab, and it’s very freeing and vibrant. There’s a shot of her sitting in the mosque alone, and she’s observing, and she’s observing those around her. They’re in traditional dress, but she’s not. I wanted to show that juxtaposition.”

Gowan credits her close collaborations not only with Tariq but also with the production designer, cinematographer, and other department heads for finding a cohesive vision for the film. “I knew that the palette that I was establishing would sit within their world,” Gowan said. “I didn’t want the characters to stand outside it, and I didn’t want them to announce themselves. Everything was about balance, and that can’t happen alone. No costume designer, no cinematographer, no production designer is an island unto themselves. We work together, and we had a great collaboration.”

“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” is currently in theaters from Orion.

entry.title: Alden Ehrenreich Has a Lot of Opinions About His Career — and About Steve Urkel
entry.summary: The Tony winner goes long with IndieWire on "Beautiful Creatures" to "Oppenheimer," "Solo" to "Hail, Caesar!," and never taking any of it for granted.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on September 15, 2016 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.]

When I meet Alden Ehrenreich for breakfast inside a Toronto hotel, it’s way too early in the morning for this kind of music. It’s the kind of music that plays over the most dramatic parts of a movie. And it’s pretty loud. It’s the kind of music that plays when a character finally reveals the truth. I now needed Ehrenreich to reveal the truth, whatever that may be. This kind of music playing for us demanded such a thing, or what were we even doing here in the first place, except being slightly annoyed by it.

Related Stories
WGA East Moves to Block AI Models from Training on Members’ Work with New Software Partner Cloak: ‘Give Agency Back to Writers’
Ryan Gosling Turned Obstacles Into Opportunities on ‘Project Hail Mary’ — with a Little Help from Julia Roberts

Ehrenreich is in Toronto in support of Anton Corbijn’s “A Talent for Murder,” which debuted at the Toronto International Film Festival earlier this week. He plays Edward, a representative for a New York City publishing house, who has been tasked with traveling to Switzerland to meet with Patricia Highsmith (Helen Mirren), to try and convince her to write a sixth Tom Ripley book. As things progress, very reluctantly at first, the pair start hatching a story idea that envisions Edward in the Tom Ripley persona. Ehrenreich points out this is a much more interesting way into that character than just it being “a Tom Ripley movie,” in which people would have their preconceived notions of what this character should be. (A path Ehrenreich has very much been down before.)

When I got to the restaurant, I didn’t know what to expect. Like, literally. I was just told “show up here at this time,” which at a film festival is really all the information that’s needed. But I didn’t know if this was going to be a quick interview where multiple journalists are shuffled in and out, or something more interesting to meet the dramatic music that was playing.

Over the course of 40 minutes, we had plenty of time to jump into a lot. From Ehrenreich’s recent Tony win for “Becky Shaw” (which I saw and was fantastic), his interpretation of his role in “Oppenheimer,” how he was told “Beautiful Creatures” would be the next “Twilight,” why he joined the MCU, and how and why he learned to stop reading about himself in the press.

Oh, and Steve Urkel. He had a lot to say about Steve Urkel.

When I arrived, I happened to be wearing a Mr. Roper t-shirt under a dress shirt and this immediately caught Ehrenreich’s attention and he asked about it…

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: The first day I wore this, a random superintendent in New York was doing some work outside and stopped me on the street and in a very serious voice said, “What a great shirt. You know, they never respected him.”

Alden Ehrenreich: Right! He relates to the super.

He relates to Mr. Roper.

He identifies as the landlord there. Yeah, that’s really funny. Crazy people with their sexual escapades. They’ve got to be stopped!

By the way, this is really dramatic music playing for 10:00 AM.

Right? This is not a room that you usually spend time in in the morning.

I feel like you need to say something profound because of the music.

Exactly.

Is it intimidating going head-to-head with Helen Mirren for an entire movie?

We did a week of rehearsal about a year in advance of shooting the movie, and she was just so lovely. I’m imagining that’s the way she is in an interview? She’s so kind of gentle and warm and soft-spoken and funny and personable…

And opinionated. Yes, I brought up “The Mosquito Coast” to her in an interview and she had some very strong opinions about the critics’ reactions to Harrison Ford playing that kind of role at the time.

Yeah. She is. but she just lets the environment be whatever it’s going to be. I just immediately really got along with her and we had a great time. Before the movie was supposed to go, it all fell apart. And then we didn’t know whether it was going to happen again. Then it happened a year later. It came back and we shot it again.

Why did it fall apart?

Just financing stuff. It was wild, because when we came back it was like let’s remember what it was we were doing a year ago…

[Our server, Amy, asks for our orders and asks if we have any allergies.]

I get in trouble with doctors because when they ask me if I have allergies, I say cyanide and they get mad. I’ve never made a doctor laugh at that.

Really? They don’t like it?

They do not.

I think it’s good. I like it. When I’m at a restaurant and they say, “Do you have any allergies?” Sometimes I say cats, which is true.

See, I’ve tried the cyanide line once at a restaurant and I got the look of scorn.

Restaurant is trickier.

And I understand, because they’re busy and they don’t have time for buffonery.

Tomfoolery.

Have you ever been at a Broadway show and it feels like the actor on stage is looking right at you and it’s really uncomfortable? You did that to me in “Becky Shaw.”

Oh, really? You were sitting up front?

Yeah, we had press tickets. In a scene in which your character is seething with rage. It’s very uncomfortable.

That’s really funny.

I don’t know if you can actually see anyone up there.

I can’t. Not until the curtain call. Technically I probably could, but I’m not. I mean, I’m avoiding it at all costs. And I try to keep my sight lines on other parts of the theater where I don’t look at somebody, because you could look down at somebody and they’re looking at their phone.

Oh, that’s rude.

It kind of takes you out of it. Yeah. I mean, I didn’t have that experience, but you want to try to, in a way, see the fourth wall that isn’t there basically.

There were literal headlines that read, “Alden Ehrenreich steals the show.” You had to know things were going well.

I had wanted to do a play for a really long time. I had this weird relationship with theater where I had a theater company in my twenties, I’m opening a theater in Los Angeles at the moment, and it’s a huge part of my life. But I’ve never done a professional play.

How’s that possible?

It just is weird. There are ones that have come around that I didn’t want to do. There are ones that I pursued that I didn’t get.

It does seem like a huge commitment.

Yes, it is that. And you do it far in advance. So you commit to a play a lot. My admiration for especially older theater actors in terms of just the physical cost and in terms of they’re really doing it for the love. Nobody’s getting rich at all. And I saw people work a lot harder for a lot less on stage than I’ve seen in many instances in film. Finding that particular play and that role, there’s just once in a while you find a role that you’re like, “I can’t wait to say this stuff. I can’t wait to do this. I know I’m this guy.” I didn’t expect it to go as well as it did necessarily…

I doubt anyone goes into it thinking, “Guess who’s getting a Tony for this?”

No. I mean, I remember when I signed up my agent being like, “And it’s kind of during award season.” So I was like, “Oof, OK.” And it’s such an interesting thing because when reviews for movies come out, like today, that will happen. I really try to avoid it and all that stuff. But when you’re in a play, you have to avoid it because you actually still have to go do it. So you are taking this gamble. If you are in something and it doesn’t go over well, it’s not like you go, “OK, on to the next one.” It’s like, “OK, another six months of this.”

Right, if a movie doesn’t go over well, you can just say, “OK, I’m in ‘Oppenheimer’ now. Here I go.”

Yeah, exactly. And the way I’ve worked has always been a little bit like a theater actor, a little bit, the way I work on roles. So it felt like, I don’t know, it just felt like I got to come into an environment that was always kind of a natural fit for me, but that I’d never experienced before.

Here’s what I noticed: When you came out for the curtain call you weren’t smiling or anything. You still looked like you were in character. You took a quick bow and got off stage.

I mean, I got that note when we were in dress rehearsal. They were like, “Try to look a little less miserable.”

Miserable’s not the word. It’s like you were still the character. But you didn’t look happy.

Totally. The emotional climax of the whole piece for my character happens 30 seconds before the play ends.

I like that you didn’t take their note.

Yeah, I think what you said is probably true. I’m still kind of in it at that point. It takes a little bit of a moment afterwards to… Little rituals and get out of it and shift gears a little bit, which is its own process that I was learning through that whole period. How do you balance your day-to-day life? It’s very different. In a movie you have a big scene on Thursday, and the hours, they’re longer. With a play, you do the whole thing, obviously, you’re living the whole story every day. And so you have more downtime, but in a way that downtime is more needed for recovery.

So you went straight from “A Talent for Murder” to “Becky Shaw” on Broadway? Is that how that worked out?

Oh, no. I went back to LA and was writing, and then we did a play reading at my theater with Robert Downey Jr. of “Our Town.”

So you got to steal some more scenes from him like in “Openheimer”?

I wasn’t in it. He was unbelievable. He played the stage manager.

But you know you did that in “Oppenheimer.” You know you got some big laughs.

I love my character.

Well, he’s great.

When I did that, I watched “Mr. Smith Goes to Washington,” because I think for all the gravitas of that movie, there’s a lot of a brooding quality to the movie. And Chris Nolan never said anything like this, but I felt a, kind of, I don’t know… almost like an old school classical sort of patriotism in the writing that I felt like Chris Nolan was moved by and mattered to him. And that was something that I felt a lot of as a kid. And obviously becomes more complicated as you grow up and as the world changes and as the country changes. But to be in that moment and get to play a character that was very much the sort of, to me, kind of a character that was in the world of a Jimmy Stewart or a person like that was very exciting.

And you got to deliver the big line about JFK and act like you have no idea who that is.

Yeah, that’s true. You have to downplay that. And even that is almost like that line I felt he’s invoking a kind of optimism. Because even though now we’ve lived so far past that moment, what Kennedy represented, the kind of hopefulness and optimism that Kennedy represented is probably comparable, in some way, to what Obama represented when he first came on the scene. It was like my character was like, “Oh, there’s a future past this era that we’re all going to move into that’s going to be a lot brighter for the country.” I’m curious how Chris Nolan actually feels about that, but there was almost a sentimental quality in a movie that feels very unsentimental at its face.

You mentioned how you always wanted to do a play, and “A Talent for Murder” is based on a play. Was this scratching that itch before you actually got to do it? I know it’s not the same. You’re not in front of a crowd.

No, it’s not, but it is sort of? I think some of the things that draw me to theater are the things that drew me to the movie because, when I read it, and I knew that Helen was doing it, it was like a little bit almost like… so, I did a movie called “Hail, Caesar!” 10 years ago or something…

I’m very familiar with “Hail, Caesar!,” yes.

So I got to do sort of…

You have one of the most famous lines of dialogue in that movie that will follow you the rest of your life. I love it when actors do that, “I did this little Coen brothers movie, ‘Hail, Caesar!’ I don’t know if you saw it or not.”

[Laughs] I don’t assume! But yes, it’s true. And that line follows me in the good times and the bad times. There’s a lot of different ways to use that line. But that felt a little bit like, oh, I would get to do this one act play with Ralph Fiennes almost inside of it. And this felt like, oh, I get to do almost a full play with Helen. Anton Corbijn is not a theater guy, but me and Helen kind of rehearsed it in the very limited amount of time we had. The way we rehearsed all that stuff was very much the way you would rehearse it if it was a play.

Can we talk about where this movie goes or not?

It’s a good question. I don’t know the answer to that. I’m happy to, but it’s really up to the people.

The way I always look at it, if it gets more people to watch it, knowing a bit where it goes…

Sure. Yeah, I think so. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with talking about it.

As the movie goes on, your character, Edward, starts envisioning a sixth Tom Ripley book with himself as Ripley. Did you know this before you read the script?

No, I didn’t know the play.

So you’re just reading the script like, “Oh, wow, this is who I’m playing?”

Exactly.

What’s that like?

Yeah. I mean, not only that, but also doing it in this way. It would be a different thing if I was just doing another Ripley thing because then it’s a much more direct comparison…

You’ve gone down that road before.

Exactly. Speaking of “The Mosquito Coast”…

Good callback.

But this is so different, because it’s basically a novel that never actually got written, that we’re working on together. And I was talking to the writer last night about this. I feel that the Ripley in this movie, even though age-wise, I’m closer to a “Talented Mr. Ripley” era, the way she wrote Ripley in the movie, in particular, feels to me more like the later Ripley novels where he’s kind of just a sociopath, basically. In the early novel, there’s a part of him that’s very wounded and some of this is coming out of rage and all this.

By the time you get to the later novels, that has been all so repressed that he’s very comfortable with himself. So I think the opportunity to do two roles — and two roles that are this different and on this different kind of spectrum? I’m trying to remember other movies and things where that happens. I mean, I know there are ones. I guess the Urkel show.

Wait, are you referencing “Family Matters”?

Yeah, exactly. He gets to play the cool version of Urkel.

Well, there’s the headline.

[Laughs] Exactly. That’s just what I was thinking. That’s going to be the headline, “Compares this to Steve Urkel.”

“Tom Ripley, he’s just like Urkel.”

Not on Urkel, on Stefan Urquelle, or whatever, you know what I mean? The cool guy version. God, I haven’t seen that show in a long time.

Jaleel White.

Yeah! That’s right. I mean, yeah, it’s a very exciting draw to get to do both of those things at the same time and figure out how to do them. And we shot basically all the Ripley stuff first in Italy, in Rome, and then did all the stuff in the room. So I had the advantage of knowing what that all feels like when I’m in the contained scenes with Helen.

At the end it tells us this is a fictional account of her life. I assume for legal reasons.

Well, you want the real legal thing?

What is it?

I’m never referred to as Ripley in the movie.

So we’re getting someone sued with this interview?

Not exactly, because I’m just a Ripley-esque character, isn’t it? But there was some back and forth with that. And I understand the people who have the rights to the book, this is not canon, this is a whole other book. It’s a whole other thing. And so there’s a fine line to draw there.

I’m going to say something controversial, but I don’t even think it’s that controversial, but I’m going to make a statement.

OK.

In your life, you will play Han Solo again.

No idea.

If you look at the way history works with all this stuff, no one expected to see Andrew Garfield as Spider-Man again. Also, last time we spoke a couple of years ago, you mentioned you felt you only got to play Han Solo as the Han we know for only about the last 15 minutes of that movie.

Oh, interesting. We’ll see.

You also joined the MCU. Was your experience good?

I liked it. I’m pretty illiterate when it comes to the MCU and how it all works or where all that all fits.

Well, you’re Jeff Bridges’ son.

Yes, that’s true. I have to remember for a second. Yeah, and I just worked with Downey when I did that, and so I called him and I was like, “Hey, what do you think of me doing this?” He was like, “Yeah, do it.” He was very encouraging and supportive and stuff, which was very nice. Shanaka Hansch, who was the showrunner, I thought had a really cool take on it and it was super interesting. And yeah, it was a kind of very easy-breezy, fun, lighthearted thing. It felt different than a movie. You throw yourself into it in the same way, but I approach it the same way I approach everything. So yeah, we’ll see if I show up there again. I don’t know.

So let me word it this way. Last time we spoke, you mentioned that of course it’s disappointing “Solo” didn’t do better. But now, smash cut, there’s you holding a Tony, big smile, “Ehrenreich steals the show.” Professionally, do you ever think, “I was kind of in a disappointing place,” compared to now where things seem to be going very well for you?

Yes.

But do you ever take stock of that?

Yeah…

Were you ever like, “Am I going to get to a place where I can even win a Tony?”

Right. I don’t know. I wasn’t really thinking that at that time. I mean…

Look, I ask this because if something bad happens to me professionally, I’m like, “Well, that’s it. I’m done.” So I can only kind of ask that based on how I’d be feeling.

Totally. I think, for me, the thing that is the most… The only thing that I can have any control over is what I show up for, which projects I choose to do, and the way I show up for them, and giving them my all in whatever way I can. And if I don’t put a wall between myself and how that ends up. For instance, later this afternoon, we’ll get the Roman — whoever’s in the stands of the coliseum will do thumbs up or thumbs down on the movie to some extent.

Yes, that’s how it works here. Some guy comes out and does a thumbs up or down after.

[Laughs] Exactly. But that’ll happen today. I have other creative stuff that I’m working on. And if I get involved with how that goes, it just kills you. To some extent, when things go well, the same thing is true. It’s like you don’t have any control over the outcomes of anything.

Is this something you had to learn not to do? When you were doing “Hail, Caesar!” And “Rules Don’t Apply,” you’re in that era, were you reading more about yourself? Because you were up and coming then. I would be tempted to be like, “Oh, things are starting to go pretty well.”

I did a movie called “Beautiful Creatures” that was supposed to be the next “Twilight.” It was not the next “Twilight.”

No, it wasn’t.

I was 22, 23. Even my first film was one of the greatest experiences of my life, maybe. But even the way that movie ended up coming out, not the movie itself. The movie itself was great and it got great press, but then when it came out, it was kind of a non-event. And so it’s been a gradual learning over the years that that side of things is just not my purview. And how well things or how poor things go changes in an instant on both cases. The main thing, honestly, the thing that I feel that’s real is I just feel really grateful that I get to work.

I know a lot of actors who can’t work, can’t get jobs, never get to have experiences like what I’m experiencing right now — going to this film festival and staying in a nice place and doing all this stuff.

Well, you’re going to get an ovation for this later.

OK, that’s nice.

You’re going to get an ovation when you walk out today.

The only way I think I can stay somewhat sane is by really focusing on whatever the next thing is and on the things that I have control over. And that’s really it. Because anytime the rest of it, even when the rest of it gets very loud, it’s just not in my control at all. And the reasons that something are successful or not almost never has anything to do with… well, I don’t know if that’s true, but all you can do is your best thing. And sometimes that comes across and sometimes it doesn’t. And there is no lesson to me other than that, really, I guess.

I interviewed Courteney Cox a couple days ago. I noticed on her Wikipedia page, after the “Friends” section, the next section was called “Continued Success.” I feel like that’s a good goal. To have that listed after a main thing.

[Laughs] Totally. Totally. The thing that I also find really reassuring is that the artists that I really love, the people who I find very, very inspiring? It’s very easy when I’m 16 reading their biographies and looking back at the whole scope of their career…

Who would this be?

Oh, I’m thinking people like Marlon Brando or John Cassavetes, where most of their career is spent in… Would be deemed like failure or disappointment, or this or that, in real time. You look at that…

Cassavetes is fascinating. Because he plays these scumbags in some movies, but then he makes “Faces.”

Exactly!

It’s insane it’s the same person.

It’s amazing. And my sense of somebody like him is his entire… Whatever the headlines were in his era were certainly not about him and about his movie being number one or about this or that or any of that. And yet, over the course of time, because he was so committed to what he was trying to do, we have this feeling about him. Because over the course of time, the flame at the center of that stayed lit. And so the short-term gain of a certain success next week can kind of cost you the integrity of a lifetime sometimes, if you chase it. And then no one really cares or remembers anyway about how the thing did or didn’t do. It really is about the thing itself.

So that’s another kind of thing I try to remember sometimes. And it’s not like… I’m presenting this like I have this perfect… I, by no means, am not vulnerable to caring or having my feelings hurt or giving a shit about these things. But, as best I can, it’s just not really useful. And at its best, it can be instructive on how to keep your focus on the stuff you do care about or get clearer about what that is.

See, I feel you met the moment right there with the dramatic music that’s playing.

I did.

That was profound.

Appreciate it. The Steve Urkel stuff probably most of all.

“A Talent for Murder” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.

entry.title: As It Readies for Boulder Debut, Sundance Institute Names Tracy Brady as Chief Marketing, Brand, and Communications Officer
entry.summary: Brady will lead the Institute’s comprehensive marketing and communications strategy as it readies for its Boulder, Colorado debut.
entry.content:
The Sundance Institute today announced the appointment of Tracy Brady as its new Chief Marketing, Brand, and Communications Officer.

Per an official release, “Brady will lead the Institute’s comprehensive marketing and communications strategy and joins the executive leadership team at a pivotal moment, taking the helm to connect the nonprofit’s diverse artist initiatives under a singular, cohesive brand vision as the Sundance Film Festival prepares for its relocation to Boulder, Colorado in 2027.”

Brady succeeds the late, great Tammie Rosen, Sundance Institute’s Chief Communications Officer, who passed away in December of 2025.

Related Stories
‘Klara and the Sun’ Review: Jenna Ortega Plays a Manic Pixie Android in Taika Waititi’s Confoundingly Awful Kazuo Ishiguro Adaptation
12 Must-See AFI Fest Movies According to the Festival’s Team, from Sexy Gay Romance ‘Flesh and Fuel’ to Animated ‘Iron Boy’

Brady’s career so far has been a wide-ranging one, and her previous experience in the entertainment industry includes roles in publicity, awards, and marketing strategy at Fox Searchlight Pictures, Sony Pictures Entertainment, and Turner Broadcasting. Most recently, Brady served as SVP of Communications and Social Impact at Green Thumb Industries, where she led enterprise-wide communications and social impact initiatives.

Brady previously built and scaled the global communications teams and efforts for Curaleaf, the largest publicly traded multi-state operator in its industry. She also served as SVP of Corporate Communications and Marketing at Hill Holiday and VP at Arnold Entertainment and Arnold Brand Promotions. Through her previous roles, she often counted the Sundance Film Festival as a client.

She is also a published novelist, essayist, an award-winning humorist, and the founder of Wit & Word, a live event series that features independent artists and writers. Brady holds a B.A. in Communications, Magna Cum Laude, from Fordham University and studied French Language and Civilization at Sorbonne University.

“Tracy is a visionary, strategic, and results-oriented marketing and communications leader,” said David Linde, CEO of the Sundance Institute, in an official statement. “As we transition to our new home in Boulder and embrace the evolving future of independent cinema, we need a trusted voice to bring our community, artists and global audience together. Tracy’s understanding of storytelling, brand marketing and strategic communications, coupled with her lifelong passion and dedication to the arts, makes her the perfect executive to guide our brand forward.”

In her new role, Brady will “be tasked with unifying the organization’s messaging and public presence, ensuring that every facet of the Sundance Institute moves forward together. As the entertainment landscape rapidly evolves, her leadership will align the Institute’s brand reputation, media relations, and digital strategy to reflect current trends in culture and independent filmmaking.”

Brady’s new mandate “centers on a holistic approach to storytelling, tying together the Institute’s impact, artist programs, and the upcoming Sundance Film Festival in Boulder to create a powerful, unified experience for artists, industry partners and audiences alike.”

“I am thrilled and honored to join the Sundance Institute during a transformative moment,” said Brady in her own statement. “As a lifelong fan of independent filmmaking and a dedicated storyteller, I have always believed in the power of artistic expression to shape culture and forge connection. As we move toward the 2027 Sundance Film Festival in Boulder, my focus will be on bringing our entire community together, both inside the Institute and out. My aim is to continue to align our communications and marketing efforts under a unified mission so we can better support artists, adapt to the dynamic changes in the entertainment industry, and ensure the Sundance Institute remains the premiere champion for independent filmmakers worldwide.”

Brady will report to Sundance Institute CEO David Linde and be based in Boulder.

entry.title: ‘Klara and the Sun’ Review: Jenna Ortega Plays a Manic Pixie Android in Taika Waititi’s Confoundingly Awful Kazuo Ishiguro Adaptation
entry.summary: Jenna Ortega stars in Taika Waititi's confoundingly awful dystopian fable 'Klara and the Sun,' adapted from Kazuo Ishiguro's novel. Review.
entry.content:
Leave your brain at the door, lest you want your IQ pulverized, if you see Taika Waititi’s confoundingly awful, relentlessly twee Kazuo Ishiguro adaptation, “Klara and the Sun.” Starring Jenna Ortega as solar-powered AF (artificial friend) Klara, whose overexposure to broad, deeply stupid human feelings starts to empower her with them, it’s this year’s “A Big Bold Beautiful Journey” — another auteur-backed misfire and unintended preamble to director jail.

Where Ishiguro, the Nobel-winning Japanese-British author of “The Remains of the Day” and “Never Let Me Go,” writes in plaintive, precise prose grounded in ambiguous emotions, Waititi fills in the spaces with pastel-popped set design, thwacks of whimsy, and gauche slapstick comedy that undermine every already-half-hearted gesture at profundity. Take a scene where two characters run to Klara’s rescue amid a burning building, only to get shocked by an electric fence at least three times, but more, I think. Michael Giacchino’s bathetic score, layered over such a bizarrely cued pratfall, crystallizes precisely the miscalculated clash of tensions felt in every frame as the movie supposedly hurtles toward a big emotional climax. “Klara and the Sun” is pathologically allergic to sincerity, treating major existential questions as treacle — and worse, uncuriously.

Related Stories
12 Must-See AFI Fest Movies According to the Festival’s Team, from Sexy Gay Romance ‘Flesh and Fuel’ to Animated ‘Iron Boy’
WGA East Moves to Block AI Models from Training on Members’ Work with New Software Partner Cloak: ‘Give Agency Back to Writers’

This latest Dystopian Future World That Reflects Our Own is comprised of what-else-but rigidly stratified class structures, bespoke genetic engineering available only to the wealthiest, and super-sentient artificial intelligence. That would be Kara, a now-obsolete B2 model android companion. She’s human on the outside, but all conductor wires and an inky, petrol-like liquid on the inside. One bug suggests she’s ready for factory recall: Klara can’t stop standing on one leg in tree pose, a glitch in her matrix and a gag that Waititi returns to again and again to absolutely no effect other than in irritating the hell out of the audience. She spends her numbered days and ways — numbered in the sense that she’s due to be shipped back to the factory for destruction — pining for the “super-duper nourishing nourishment” of the slats of sunlight slipping through the grille separating the shop from the city center.

When the shutters come up and Store Manager (Natasha Lyonne as, I believe, herself) opens the shop, Klara and her android cohorts must strike a pose, dance-monkey-dance style, in the window to allure potential buyers to take them. But they’re already dazzled and distracted by the shiny newness of the Looksmaxxed model B3s across the street. Lucky for Klara, a very lonely, very sick girl named Josie (Mia Tharia) wants to buy her, much to the chagrin of her dismissive, martinet of a mother, Chrissie (Amy Adams, in yet another role that’s… what’s the opposite of plum?).

Josie and her single mom live on a middle-of-nowhere farm where the biggest threat (and, apparently, the movie’s arch villain) is a self-driving crop harvester manufactured by a company called Cootings. Josie is an only child who’s been “Lifted,” meaning her genetic makeup has been altered to retrofit what must’ve been an underachieving streak into a stroke of genius. She paints masterpieces and reads the great novels, day and night, as Chrissie readies her daughter for the Atlas Brookings school of gifted children. (Though when we meet her classmates, they’re all dullards with speech affectations and severely over-swaddled, sleeping-bag-like couture.)

Klara, whose philosophical raptures treat the Sun as a living deity and who is also capable of parroting any human’s voice or temperament on command, becomes fast friends with the girl. But the Lifting procedure has stricken Josie with some sort of unspecified neurological disorder that gets activated when the duo and Josie’s friend Rick (Aran Murphy) take a joyride in Chrissie’s self-driving Buick. One minute they’re flying through the fields with mirthful abandon, the next, smash cut to the car in a tree, and Josie in a coma in bed with tubes attached. The capricious shift is whiplash-inducing, as if editors Adam Gough and Tom Eagles cleaved a sizable chunk of footage from the film. Or are Waititi and co-writer Dahvi Waller deliberately obfuscating as some kind of middle finger to the audience? Really, you’re left wondering what just happened, and every cutaway to Klara’s literally juddering first-person viewpoint (which Josie also appears to share) doesn’t help clarify any of the narrative muddlement.

Steve Buscemi plays a Dr. Frankenstein type who holds the key to unlocking whatever’s medically afoot with Josie, and to Chrissie keeping her daughter alive if the girl doesn’t make it through the next nosebleed. From there, “Klara and the Sun” devolves into a kind of kooky pas de deux between Chrissie and Klara as Josie convalesces. At one point, as a fed-up Chrissie tries to shove Klara back into the deteriorating cardboard box from whence the girl came, she barks at Klara to “upsy-daisy” and get out of the box when it won’t close. “Who’s Daisy?” Klara asks. The film’s pick-me jabs at humor are frankly, flatly unfunny and grating, twisting the film at times into a perverse, almost self-aware treatise on tweeness. But that would be giving the movie too much intellectual credit.

The New Zealand actor and filmmaker is never an artist who takes the material too seriously. See how he turned fascism into Oscar-minted farce with Best Adapted Screenplay winner “Jojo Rabbit.” Here, his clumsy, winky, affected, and self-undercutting direction can’t even work the charming Jenna Ortega to a great performance, as her Klara is flattened into a bundle of manic pixie mannerisms both physical and verbal.

Ortega’s plenty magnetic on Netflix’s “Wednesday,” but her streak of recent film roles — from Sundance’s grueling art-world satire “The Gallerist” to the disastrous Weeknd vehicle “Hurry Up Tomorrow” and A24’s busted monster franchise-nonstarter “Death of a Unicorn” — suggests her talents are being staggeringly misapplied on the big screen. (“If I Had Legs I’d Kick You” writer/director Mary Bronstein, however, is hopefully coming to the rescue with her next movie.) For a movie filled with self-driving cars and powered by artificial intelligence, this “Klara” goes nowhere but straight into the sun of disaster, and without intelligence of any kind.

Grade: D

“Klara and the Sun” opens in theaters starting Friday, October 23.

entry.title: 12 Must-See AFI Fest Movies According to the Festival’s Team, from Sexy Gay Romance ‘Flesh and Fuel’ to Animated ‘Iron Boy’
entry.summary: AFI Fest programmers pick must-see features and shorts from this year's festival, running October 21-25 in Los Angeles.
entry.content:
AFI Fest returns to Los Angeles this week, starting Thursday, October 22, with the U.S. premiere of Laika Studios’ long-awaited animated feature “Wildwood” opening the festival. The festival is an annual opportunity to catch the best from the global festival circuit — especially as Oscar campaign season readies for November.

Highlights include IndieWire favorite and Venice Silver Lion winner “Possible Love,” directed by Lee Chang-dong; Ryûsuke Hamaguchi’s Cannes prize-winning “All of a Sudden,” starring Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto; Werner Herzog’s wily fantasy comedy “Bucking Fastard,” starring Kate Mara and Rooney Mara; Andrew Haigh’s “A Long Winter,” starring Fred Hechinger, Kit Connor, Ebon Moss-Bachrach and Caitríona Balfe; Mike Leigh’s San Sebastián Golden Shell winner “Tender Loving Care”; and the North American premiere of Céline Sciamma’s “Tutti Frutti,” which premiered earlier this year at the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

Related Stories
WGA East Moves to Block AI Models from Training on Members’ Work with New Software Partner Cloak: ‘Give Agency Back to Writers’
Ryan Gosling Turned Obstacles Into Opportunities on ‘Project Hail Mary’ — with a Little Help from Julia Roberts

But beneath the hood of the buzzier titles are plenty of lesser-sung selections worth your time, and a ticket. Below, IndieWire polled the AFI Fest programmers for their favorite films out of the features and shorts sections to help guide your long weekend at the movies. See the festival website for ticket info and full descriptions. The festival runs through October 25.

Features

Todd Hitchcock, Director, AFI FEST
“The Idiot(s)”
I am an unapologetic fan of biopics and period pieces, but these genres can tend toward weighty over-seriousness. How refreshing then to see what Polish filmmakers Małgorzata Szumowska and Michał Englert have done with “The Idiot(s)”, their cheeky, spoofy take on Fyodor Dostoyevsky (Johnny Flynn) and his wife Anna’s (Aimee Lou Wood) honeymoon in Baden-Baden, when the great writer was supposed to be hard at work fulfilling a contract to write “The Idiot,” but instead wasted his time doing anything but, chiefly gambling and losing big. Englert also supervised the stunning cinematography, and one marvels at how this often silly film looks so smart. Fans of Yorgos Lanthimos’ “The Favourite” and “Poor Things” will find much to like.

Abbie Algar, Director, Programming
“Mouse”
Contemporary masters of humane cinema Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson follow “Saint Francis” and “Ghostlight” with “Mouse,” a tender, bittersweet, and deeply truthful coming-of-age drama set in 2002 Arkansas. When shy theater kid Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer, who also starred in “Ghostlight” alongside her parents) loses her charismatic best friend Callie (Chloe Coleman), she forms an unexpected bond with Callie’s mother, Helen (Sophie Okonedo). This unconventional, generation-spanning bond opens a path through grief, love and self-discovery that gives the film a wholly unexpected arc. Eschewing and subverting teen drama tropes, “Mouse” finds its emotional power in the naturalistic performances of its stellar ensemble cast, an indelible sense of time and place and a warmth and humor that affirm O’Sullivan and Thompson’s rare gift for finding hope in humanity.

Screening to be followed by a conversation with director and screenwriter Kelly O’Sullivan, director and producer Alex Thompson and actors Sophie Okonedo, Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Tara Mallen.

Josh Gardner, Senior Programmer
“9 Temples to Heaven”
A meditative travelogue, Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s narrative feature debut finds a family making pilgrimage to nine Buddhist temples in a single day to bring good fortune to their skeptical matriarch. A revelation in the Directors’ Fortnight sidebar at the Cannes Film Festival, this simple setup uncovers existential truth about contemporary conceptions of mortality and spirituality. These ideas sparked my weary soul, fueled by both the deeply universal script and Chidgasornpongse’s formal control of his images, both mundane and surreal. A longtime collaborator of Thai auteur Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Chidgasornpongse’s narrative feature debut is Thailand’s Oscar submission for Best International Feature.

Javier Chavez, Programmer
“Iron Boy”
“Iron Boy” is an absolutely gorgeous film; so much of the pleasure of watching it is seeing the watercolor aesthetic in motion, loosely drawn ink lines wrapped around the characters. This style gives the rural French countryside a dreamy look, as if it were a cherished memory (in fact, filmmaker Louis Clichy drew on his personal life for the film). It serves a specific yet universal tale of acceptance and finding one’s place in the world — especially for children, but adults will connect with this inspiring story, too.

Mimi Brody, Programmer
“Flesh and Fuel”
One of the unexpected pleasures of my festival viewing this year was Pierre Le Gall’s “Flesh and Fuel,” an unconventional romance that completely won me over. Set in the unglamorous world of European long-haul trucking, it follows two men, Étienne, a veteran French driver, and Bartosz, a Polish trucker, whose casual hookup develops into an unexpected romance. Sexually frank, funny and surprisingly tender, the film features two terrific performances by Alexis Manenti and Julian Świeżewski, whose earthy, lived-in sensuality is a refreshing departure from conventional screen romance — and idealized male leads. I found myself completely invested in these two men and their unlikely romance, which was both refreshingly unsentimental and deeply affecting.

Screening to be followed by a conversation with director and screenwriter Pierre Le Gall.

Anna Li, Programmer:
“At Night”
Watching Beatrice Gibson’s feature debut “At Night” is a transfixing, magical experience — for 87 minutes, you wander the dimly lit Parisian streets, popping in and out of sparsely populated bars and Metro stations, observing the nocturnal conversations among a community of women. Women who are poets, academics, sex workers, intellectuals and artists, who are open and frank with each other, who muse on the texts of feminist literary figures like June Jordan and Alice Notley and in the same breath chat about their sexual insecurities. Recalling Akerman’s late-70s output, its analog ambiance and melancholy, almost Lynchian in its quiet liminality, and its languid drift in a unique autofiction form, I never wanted the night to end.

Travis Weedon, Associate Programmer
“Forever Your Maternal Animal”
Valentina Maurel’s tempestuous sophomore feature was the discovery of Cannes for me. I left the theater vibrating, coming down from more than just a well-placed Alice Coltrane needle drop. The three leads rightly received Best Actress honors in the Un Certain Regard section for their raw portrayal of the headstrong women at the center of an unraveling middle-class family in San José, Costa Rica. Fractured families are hardly untrodden cinematic ground, but Maurel manages a rare and transporting feat of performance, perspective and poetry, as she fleetly wends her way through the family’s knotty dynamic with lyrical direction and an empathy that never shortchanges the humanity of her characters.

Screening to be followed by a conversation with director and screenwriter Valentina Maurel.

Natalia Ames, Associate Programmer
“The Meltdown”
Can a country undergo an authentic transformation in the name of modernity and openness, or is its forced rebranding merely a whitewash, concealing its most painful truths? “The Meltdown,” Manuela Martelli’s follow-up to “Chile ’76” and her country’s Oscar submission for Best International Feature, explores these questions about Chile in the early 1990s, in the aftermath of Pinochet’s era. The film follows a young girl (stunning newcomer Maya O’Rourke) who, much like the audience, must piece together a puzzle of scattered information, covered-up truths and blatant lies in order to make sense of a new reality.

Screening to be followed by a conversation with director and screenwriter Manuela Martelli and producer Alejandra García.

Eli Prysant, Assistant Programmer
“Goodbye Cruel World”
As a fan of 2014’s “Eden,” my interest was immediately piqued when I heard its lead Félix de Givry would be making his directorial debut, and “Goodbye Cruel World” did not disappoint. Capturing the magic of young love where the connection between you seems to create your own special world, Givry’s film is keenly observed and a promising sign of hopefully more films to come.

Shorts

Nichole Young, Short Film Programmer & Programming Coordinator
“Chuuraa”
Screens as part of Shorts Program: Documentary 2
Descend into the icy depths of the Siberian underworld in Oscar-nominated Evgenia Arbugaeva’s latest documentary, “Churraa.” Guided by Indigenous Sakha paleontologist Aisin, we traverse through the labyrinthine permafrost in search of an ancient creature. Plunge into this immersive epic, uncovering what chilling relics risk escaping the thawing ice. Arbugaeva’s haunting soundscape and claustrophobic cinematography transcend the mythological realm and natural world; illuminated by a single torch, we rediscover just how minuscule and fragile the human race is. Don’t miss this cinematic marvel that must be experienced on the big screen!

Payton Ewalt, Associate Programmer, Short Films
“Trading Cards”
Screens as part of Shorts Program: Animation 1
Would you steal away the innocence of your childhood for a moment of peace in your present? Visionary Radheya Jang centers the conversation of self-discovery and mental health around the media we surrounded ourselves with as children. Here, the richness of color, sound and narration coalesce into a poetic introspection that can only be described as divine. Swelling with magic and atmosphere, “Trading Cards” aims directly at the young heart and pierces through the warmth of nostalgia to haunt it with the omnipresent anxieties of the future.

Daniel Crooke, Associate Programmer, Short Films
“The Bovine Comedy”
Screens as part of Shorts Program: After Dark
Words will fail to capture the unexpected essence which director Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke spills into being with this follow-up work to his breakout feature debut “A Useful Ghost”(AFI Fest 2025). This is a filmmaker fully in command of where to place his camera and what to put inside of his frame, balancing a confrontational hook with a gentle human touch. The plainspoken ways he brings his futuristic setting to life are remarkable, given how unremarkable they may seem to his characters, who are simply living their ordinary lives in a world that, at first glance, may feel unordinary to the viewer. If it seems like I’m avoiding a description of the plot, it’s because I am!

entry.title: WGA East Moves to Block AI Models from Training on Members’ Work with New Software Partner Cloak: ‘Give Agency Back to Writers’
entry.summary: The Writers Guild of America East is partnering with Cloak, a software program that makes scripts unreadable to AI models, preventing training.
entry.content:
The Writers Guild of America, East unveiled a partnership to help prevent AI models from training off of its members’ work on Tuesday. The software program Cloak, which creates copies of files that are illegible to AI models but readable for humans, will be available for free to WGAE members as part of the union’s benefits program. The encryption tool will protect writers from their work being exploited by AI without their consent.

“The WGAE partnership with Cloak expands our efforts to protect members’ work and fight back against AI companies exploiting writers and other creative workers,” WGA East president Tom Fontana said in a statement unveiling the partnership. “Members don’t need to worry that their work will be used to train AI models after they send it to producers or agents — or simply that the product of weeks, months, or years of work will be reduced to an AI-generated summary of an email attachment.”

Related Stories
Ryan Gosling Turned Obstacles Into Opportunities on ‘Project Hail Mary’ — with a Little Help from Julia Roberts
‘Clayface’ Introduces DC Studios’ Gotham City — but Director James Watkins Never Felt Pressure to Set Up Future Films

In addition to being provided as a free service to those within the WGAE, writers who aren’t members can add Cloak by registering their script through the guild’s website. The cost to add Cloak protection is $10 for non-members, on top of other pre-existing registration fees.

“For the past three years, the assumption was that anything you put out onto the internet is at risk of being ingested by AI, so I developed Cloak as a way to give agency back to writers to protect against unwanted AI training, AI notes, and analysis,” said Cloak founder Rishi Ambavanekar. “Until now, there hasn’t been a real technically-sound way to fight back against AI and determine how the content you create actually interacts with it. I hope Cloak can keep creative writing in the hands of people and not as data being processed by machines. I want to thank the WGAE and look forward to seeing writers have more confidence in sharing their work far and wide.”

AI’s capacity to dramatically alter and diminish the labor force within the entertainment industry has become an existential concern over recent years. The WGAE and other guilds have sought to include language addressing protections from AI in new union contracts. The Cloak partnership is a product of the guild’s AI Task Force.

“Generative AI models are often falsely advertised on the promise that they will make our work obsolete, but the truth is, the creative process is human and always will be,” said Larry J. Cohen, co-chair of the AI Task Force. “That’s why the guild is advocating for better protections against and awareness of the risks posed by AI — not just through our contracts, but through legislation and member education. Our partnership with Cloak is a natural and necessary extension of our fight to protect our members’ creative rights and the integrity of their work.”

Founded in September 2025, Cloak is backed by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz’s start-up accelerator program Speedrun and the University of Pennsylvania, per the company’s LinkedIn page. The start-up’s website claims that recent tests have proven “effective” against Anthropic’s Claude model up to Fable 5.1, Google’s Gemini model up to 3.8, and OpenAI’s ChatGPT model up to GPT-6 Astra, as well as against automated summaries generated by Google Drive, Gmail, and Adobe Acrobat.

entry.title: Ryan Gosling Turned Obstacles Into Opportunities on ‘Project Hail Mary’ — with a Little Help from Julia Roberts
entry.summary: The star of Phil Lord and Chris Miller's sci-fi hit talks about his attraction to Andy Weir's novel, how he acted opposite a rock alien, and more.
entry.content:
Back in 2020, “The Martian” author Andy Weir sent Ryan Gosling a manuscript that hadn’t yet been published, but which he hoped the actor would respond to. When Gosling read “Project Hail Mary,” the story of a science teacher tasked with saving the world and stranded in space with only a rock-like alien for company, he felt exactly the way Weir had hoped.

“It felt like this project had a knife in my ribs,” Gosling told me at a Q&A I moderated following a guild screening of the film. “When I put the book down, the knife was saying, ‘OK, now you’re going to call [Phil] Lord and [Chris] Miller, and you’re going to get them to direct this. Then you’re going to get [producer] Amy Pascal to help you, and then you’re going to try to put together the best team there is in the business.’ It just took me hostage.”

Related Stories
‘Clayface’ Introduces DC Studios’ Gotham City — but Director James Watkins Never Felt Pressure to Set Up Future Films
RIP Ann Hornaday, a Newspaper Film Critic Survivor

Six years later, “Project Hail Mary” is one of the biggest critical and commercial hits of 2026 and Gosling is a frontrunner for a well-deserved Oscar nomination. It’s hard to think of many other films of this scale that are so entirely dependent on one actor to do all the heavy lifting. Gosling is in every scene of the 156-minute movie, and he’s called upon to play every note on the tonal scale in a performance that utilizes his razor-sharp comic timing before moving into emotionally devastating registers.

What makes the work all the more impressive is that Gosling has to do all of it without benefit of a scene partner; aside from some flashback scenes depicting his character back on earth, he spends the entire movie with only the alien “Rocky” to act opposite. Luckily, Lord and Miller dismissed the idea of creating Rocky as an entirely computer-generated figure and insisted on having an actor and puppeteer on set to play the alien.

“I don’t think anyone else would have done that,” he said. “It was definitely the much harder route, and this was already very difficult. But it was their first instinct, and it was exactly why I wanted to work with them. I just knew that it didn’t matter how hard it was going to be, they were going make these choices because they were right, and they appreciate that the obstacles are opportunities.”

Those obstacles were plentiful on the set, since the Rocky puppet was often breaking or malfunctioning. “It was like the ‘Jaws’ shark,” he said. “Sometimes just the finger would work.” Rocky was played by James Ortiz, an actor with extensive puppeteering experience who impressed Gosling at his initial audition. There was an immediate rapport, and when Ortiz left the audition Gosling called after him, “Bye, Rocky!”

The problem was that on set it was no longer just Ortiz and Gosling. “It was six puppeteers, dressed like ninjas, and me pretending I couldn’t see them,” he said. Luckily, like Lord and Miller, Ortiz also saw problems and mistakes as opportunities, which Gosling felt mirrored the subject of the film. “We’re all working together to figure out the problem, and it’s what the characters are going through. They’re trying to solve problems so that they can move on with their mission.”

One of Rocky’s most charming attributes, for example, came about because the puppet wasn’t working. “They couldn’t get the arm to turn around to give a thumbs up,” he said. “So we were just like, ‘Let’s go with it,’ and that’s why the puppet gives a thumbs down.” Which isn’t to say that the problem solving was all fun, or Gosling never got tired of the constant challenges.

“I had been acting for a long time on the film, and gone through a lot of incarnations of the character, and really felt like I had tried everything I could think of,” he said. “I had been in a placenta onesie. I looked like a space caveman. I acted like I was born. I acted like I didn’t know how to talk. I was a toddler. I was a man. And by the end of it, we got to this very expensive set, which was all these LED screens we had been waiting for to be built. We invested a lot of money in that, and it was very visually beautiful and fancy and high-tech. But I was just so tired of acting alone.”

Gosling went outside for some air, and saw Julia Roberts. “I’d never met her, and she sat down and talked to me,” he said. “She was talking about how much fun she was having on her set with Luca Guadagnino on ‘After the Hunt.’ She said, ‘You should come over,’ and I needed human interaction. So I went down to the set, and they were shooting a party scene, and they were all drinking and having fun, and they seemed like they were having a great time.”

When Gosling returned to the “Project Hail Mary” set, he told Lord and Miller he was tired of acting alone. “I said, ‘I want a friend, I want someone to act with,'” he said. “They were like, ‘OK, but what do we do?’ And I said, ‘I want to get a mop, and I want to make it into a person and talk to it.’ And they stopped everything on our fancy, expensive day, and crawled around the sets looking for tape and glasses, and a dress. And they helped me build this mop lady for me to do scenes with, who we called Moppy Ringwald.”

As Gosling sees it, the fact that Lord and Miller stopped everything to make that happen is emblematic of why the film worked. “What were supposed to be these great visual scenes with all these LEDs, it was just a mop and sunglasses, and they put it in the movie.” In addition to realizing how important that kind of spontaneity could be, Gosling learned something else as well. “If you’re having a problem and you can’t solve it, talk to Julia Roberts. That’s the big lesson here. She’ll solve it for you.”

“Project Hail Mary” is currently streaming on Prime Video.

entry.title: ‘Clayface’ Introduces DC Studios’ Gotham City — but Director James Watkins Never Felt Pressure to Set Up Future Films
entry.summary: 'Clayface' director James Watkins tells IndieWire about his new DC Comics origin story.
entry.content:
“Clayface” represents quite a few milestones for James Gunn and Peter Safran’s tenure running DC Studios. An R-rated horror movie about a minor Batman villain, the film is the first true test of their thesis that DC Comics mythology is diverse and complex enough to support a wide range of films in completely different genres. Its creative team has some serious horror bona fides: the film was pitched by Mike Flanagan, who wrote the original script that remained largely intact after revisions by Hossein Amini; and directed by none other than James Watkins, whose filmography includes spooky hits like “The Woman in Black” and “Speak No Evil.” But most notable of all, perhaps, is the fact that “Clayface” gives us our first look at the DC Studios take on Gotham City.

Related Stories
RIP Ann Hornaday, a Newspaper Film Critic Survivor
Curry Barker on Why Gen Z Loves Going to the Movies: ‘It’s Social Interaction, but You’re Not Expected to Talk to Anyone’

The fictional urban epicenter that houses Batman and his many foes is the ultimate backdrop for comic book filmmaking. Directors ranging from Tim Burton to Christopher Nolan have each put their own distinct visual spin on the urban setting. And while Gunn and Safran have not announced a Batman of their own (the Matt Reeves/Robert Pattinson series is continuing, but exists separately from their interconnected universe), everyone knows it’s coming at some point. After almost two decades of cinematic universes dominating Hollywood, it would be fair to assume that every second of this film’s take on the city would be meticulously supervised to set up future projects.

But that couldn’t be further from Watkins’ experience. During a recent conversation with IndieWire on the Warner Bros. lot, the British director opened up about making his first comic book movie. As he tells it, working with some of the most valuable IP on the planet didn’t meaningfully change his filmmaking process.

“There weren’t mandates, there was no ‘You need to do this, you need to do that,'” Watkins said of designing his take on Gotham. “I’ve got a very, very, very brilliant production designer, James Price, he did ‘Poor Things,’ he won an Oscar. And we worked trying to design what we felt was the right version of Gotham for our story. This kind of overbearing, overpowering, the cities dominating the people, the slightly retro feel of it. We looked a lot of photography from New York, from the ’70s, ’80s and ’90s, and tried to copy that in the light, and in the neons, and in the slightly dirty poetry of it. And so we just presented it and said ‘This is what we’re going to do,’ and people were excited by it.”

The process may not have been as seamless in every franchise, but Watkins credits the environment that Gunn and Safran have fostered at DC Studios, which prioritizes supporting filmmakers and treating each project as an individual work of art rather than a piece in a larger puzzle.

“I pitched my version of the movie and everybody signed up, and everyone was like, ‘Yeah, we all are aligned, we’re into this,'” he said. “It was just an incredibly supportive atmosphere of how to achieve it. They wanted to lean into that, and I think they try to be filmmaker-driven and they trusted me. And it was great… If you try and do things algorithmically, I just don’t think it works. People can smell it, or it just feels engineered in some way. It’s got to come from passion, it’s got to come from point of view, it’s got to come from ‘Here’s a story idea and a character idea that we’re chasing.'”

In this case, that story idea was a man with a face that might as well be clay. More specifically, it’s the story of Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), an actor whose one night stand with a mob wife makes him a powerful enemy. It isn’t long before the Gotham mob hacks up his face with a switchblade and spreads a series of false rumors that end his promising acting career and leave him with a hopeless future. His only hope is an experimental treatment developed by Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), which restores his money-making face but brings some unintended consequences. Matt might be beautiful on the surface again, but the vengeance in his heart and his newfound ability to shapeshift lead him down a tragic path towards becoming one of Gotham’s fiercest villains.

Watkins explained that he was drawn to the multifaceted nature of Flanagan’s script, which allowed him to incorporate Cronenberg-inspired creature design and old school effects (whenever Matt’s face isn’t moving, it’s practical), body-switching comedy (almost everyone in the cast eventually gets to play Clayface for a scene or two), and a classically dark corruption arc for the titular antihero.

“Obviously there was the body horror. But it was also a grounded, character-led origin story,” he said. “I don’t like just doing clockwork horror, I like the sense of a story that comes from character, comes from emotion. And so, the journey between him and between Matt Hagen and Caitlyn Corr, and their connection and the sort of weird love story of it all, the love triangle, the heartbreak, the tragedy… Matt is this guy that’s traumatized, that repressed pain comes back. So, I just took Mike’s script, and it was all there. It was just bringing out and just refining and bringing those things out.”

Much of the initial discourse around “Clayface” will revolve around how we classify it. Is it really a horror movie, or just a Batman villain movie with a bit more gore? Everyone will have to answer that question for themselves, but Watkins isn’t losing sleep over it. Much like beauty, genres are only skin deep — but the storytelling principles beneath the surface don’t change.

“I don’t know that it was that different. For me, even though it’s a comic book universe, it’s still real people,” he said. “I’m trying to keep it grounded, trying to keep within the emotion of those characters, trying to understand where they’re coming from, what they want. The more we can get under the skin of the people, I think the more you get under the skin of the horror as well.”

A Warner Bros. release, “Clayface” opens in theaters on Friday, October 23.
